text:
Yes, but only some models can, and a basic power station won't protect a computer from a sudden outage.

**What to look for**
- **Documented UPS/EPS mode with automatic switchover.** Without it, a power station may keep appliances running but still cut power to a computer or NAS during an outage ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/can-a-portable-power-station-be-used-as-a-ups)).
- **Transfer time.** Anker says 10 ms or 20 ms is fast but not 0 ms, so check your device's manual. A true online (double-conversion) UPS is the safer choice if the device needs 0 ms transfer ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/home-power-backup/portable-power-station-ups-home-server-nas)). EcoFlow warns that many products advertised as UPS take 20-30 ms or more ([EcoFlow](https://www.ecoflow.com/us/blog/use-portable-power-station-as-ups-power-supply)).
- **Pure sine wave output**, enough continuous wattage for your whole setup, and support for pass-through use ([Anker SOLIX](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/can-a-portable-power-station-be-used-as-a-ups)). Pass-through charging alone is not UPS protection.

**Examples with published specs**
- [Anker SOLIX S2000](https://www.ankersolix.com/blogs/portable-power-station/can-a-portable-power-station-be-used-as-a-ups): 2,010 Wh, 1,500 W pure sine wave, 10 ms UPS switchover, listed at $699.99 after coupon. This link goes to Anker's article, which has a "Shop Now" button, but I don't have a direct product URL.
- [EcoFlow RIVER 3 Plus](https://www.ecoflow.com/us/blog/use-portable-power-station-as-ups-power-supply): 600 W AC output, switchover under 10 ms per EcoFlow. This link also goes to the article, not a store page.

**Caveats**
- These sources are all written by the brands selling the products, so treat the claims as marketing until you check the spec sheet or manual.
- EcoFlow's article lists the DELTA Pro 3 as ">10ms" UPS, which looks like a typo or an inconsistency. Confirm the figure on the product page.
- Strong claims, like 30 ms damaging a computer, are probably overstated. Most desktop power supplies tolerate brief gaps, but check yours.
- Most of the other models I found, such as the BLUETTI and ALLPOWERS units on [Dealectric](https://dealectric.com/), had no UPS specs in these results, so I can't say whether they work as a UPS.

**How to size it**
Runtime in hours ≈ battery Wh × inverter efficiency (~0.85) ÷ load in watts. A 1,000 Wh unit running a 100 W setup lasts roughly 8.5 hours in ideal conditions. Measure your computer's real draw with a plug-in watt meter.

**Bottom line:** For a desktop with no strict 0 ms requirement, a power station with a documented UPS mode of 10 ms or less is reasonable. If you run a server, a NAS holding important data, or anything with a 0 ms requirement, a regular online UPS is safer. Tell me your computer's wattage and how many hours of backup you want, and I can narrow it down.
